name: Nicarchus
bio: Nicarchus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century AD.
This archive carries the 5 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book V: 38, 39, 40; Book VI: 31, 285).

poems.title: Book V, 38
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A fine and largely built woman attracts me, Similus, whether she be in her prime, or elderly. If she be young she will clasp me, if she be old and wrinkled, me fellabit.

poems.title: Book V, 39
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Must I not die? What care I if I go to Hades with gouty legs or in training for a race? I shall have many to carry me; so let me become lame, if I wish. As far as that goes, as you see, I am quite easy, and never miss a banquet.

poems.title: Book V, 40
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Don’t listen to your mother, Philumena; for once I am off and out of the town, pay no attention to those who make fun of us, but give them tit for tat, and try to be more successful than I was. Leave no stone unturned, make your own living, and write and tell me what pleasances you have visited. Try and behave with propriety. If you have anything over, pay the rent and get a coat for me. If you get with child, bring it to the birth, I entreat you. Don’t be troubled about that: when it grows up it will find out who its father was.

poems.title: Book VI, 31
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.note: Paton marks the attribution with a query.
poems.text: I nave offered this as a common gift to Pan the goattreader, to Dionysus the giver of good fruit, and to Demeter the Earth-goddess, and I beg from them fine flocks, good wine and to gather good grain from the ears.

poems.title: Book VI, 285
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.note: Paton marks the attribution with a query.
poems.text: Nicarete, who formerly was in the service of Athene’s shuttle, and stretched out many a warp on the loom, made in honour of Cypris a bonfire in front of her house of her work-basket and bobbins and her other gear, crying, “Away with ye, starving work of wretched women, that have power to waste away the bloom of youth.” Instead the girl chose garlands and the lyre, and a gay life spent in revel and festivity. “Cypris,” she said, “I will pay thee tithe of all my gains. Give me work and take from it thy due.”

poems.title: Book VII, 159
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Orpheus won the highest prize among mortals by his harp, Nestor by the skill of his sweet-phrased tongue, divine Homer, the learned in lore, by the art of his verse, but Telephanes, whose tomb this is, by the flute.

poems.title: Book IX, 330
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A. “I am goat-footed Pan, whom Simo put up by the clear waters of the spring.” B. “And why?” A. “I will tell thee. From the fountain drink as much as thou wilt, and take this hollow pitcher, too, and draw. But offer not the crystalline gifts of the Nymphs to thy feet to bathe them. Seest thou not my menacing form?” B. “Revered god—” A. “Thou shalt not speak another word, but shalt let me take my will of thee. Such is the custom of Pan. But if thou dost it! on purpose, having an inclination for the penalty, I know another trick. I will break thy head with my club.”

poems.title: Book IX, 576: On a Statue of Athena holding an Apple. Aphrodite speaks
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Trito-born maiden, why dost thou vex me now by grasping in thy hand my prize of which thou hast robbed me. Thou rememberest how formerly, amid the rocks of Ida, Paris pronounced me fairest, not thee. Thine are the spear and shield, but mine is the apple. For the apple that old war was surely enough.

poems.title: Book XI, 1
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: At the feast of Hermes, Aphrodisius, as he was carrying six choes of wine, stumbled and threw us into deep mourning. ‘“ Wine was the death even of the Centaurs.” Would it had been ours; but now it is it we have lost.

poems.title: Book XI, 7
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: No one, Charidemus, can constantly sleep with his own wife and take heart-felt pleasure in it. Our nature is so fond of titillation, such a luster after foreign flesh, that it persists in seeking the illusion of a strange caze.

poems.title: Book XI, 17
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Stephanus was poor and a gardener, but now having got on well and become rich, he has suddenly turned into Philostephanus, adding four fine letters to the original Stephanus, and in due time he will be Hippocratippiades or, owing to his extravagance, Dionysiopeganodorus. But in all the market he is still Stephanus.

poems.title: Book XI, 18
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Philaenis without conceiving bore a girl child to Heliodorus spontaneously, and when he was vexed at its being a girl she let six days pass and said she had borne a boy. So it is all over with Bubastis ; for if every woman is brought to bed like Philaenis, ' who will pay any attention to the goddess?

poems.title: Book XI, 71
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: NIconor was once in her prime, I admit that, but her prime was when Deucalion looked on the vast waters. Of those times we have no knowledge, but of her now we know that she should seek not a husband, but a tomb.

poems.title: Book XI, 73
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A handsome old woman (why deny it?) you know she was, when she was young; but then she asked for money while now she is ready to pay her mount. You will find her an artist, and when she has had something to drink then all the more you will have her submissive to whatever you want. For she drinks, if you consent, three or four pints, and then things are all topsy-turvy with her; she clings, she scratches, she plays the pathic; and if one gives her anything, she accepts, if not, the pleasure is her payment.

poems.title: Book XI, 74
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Turn out that stone-deaf old woman, Onesimus, for God’s sake, she is such a nuisance tome. If we tell her to bring soft cheeses (turot), she comes not with cheeses, but with fresh grains of wheat (purot). The other day I had a headache and asked her for rue (peganon) and she brought me an earthenware frying-pan (teganon) ; if I ask her for she brings me a rafter; if I say when I am hungry, “ Give me some greens ’”’ (lachanon), she at once brings a night-stool (lasanon). If I ask for vinegar (oxon), she brings me a bow (foxon), and if I ask for a bow, she brings vinegar ; in fact she does not comprehend a word I say. It would disgrace me to become a crier all for the sake of the old woman, and to get up at night and practise outside the town.

poems.title: Book XI, 82
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Charmus in Arcadia in the long race with five others came in (wonderful to say, but it is a fact) seventh. “As there were six,’ you will probably say, “how seventh?” A friend of his came in his overcoat calling out “Go it, Charmus,” so that thus he ran in seventh and if he had had five more friends, Zoilus, he would have come in twelfth.

poems.title: Book XI, 96
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: The birds of Stymphalus vexed not so the Arcadians, as those dead thrushes vexed me with their dry bones, very harpies, ten of them, a dry drachma’s-worth. Out on you, wretched creatures, true bats of the fields.

poems.title: Book XI, 110
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Three thin men were competing the other day about thinness, to see which of them would be adjudged the very thinnest. The one, Hermon, exhibited great skill and went through the eye of a needle holding the thread. But Demas coming out of a hole stopped at a spider’s web, and the spider spinning hung him from it. But Sosipater exclaimed, “ Give me the prize, for I lose it if I am seen, since I am nothing but air.”

poems.title: Book XI, 111
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Lean Diophantus once wishing to hang himself took a thread from a spider’s web and did so.

poems.title: Book XI, 112
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Before he anoints your eyes, Demostratus, say “ Adieu dear light,” so successful is Dion. Not only did he blind Olympicus, but through his treatment of him put out the eyes of the portrait of himself he had.

poems.title: Book XI, 113
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: The physician Marcus laid his hand yesterday on the stone Zeus, and though he is of stone and Zeus he is to be buried to-day.

poems.title: Book XI, 114
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: The astrologer Diophantus told Hermogenes the doctor that he had only nine months to live, and he, smiling, said, “ You understand what Saturn says will happen in nine months, but my treatment is more expeditious for you.”” Having said so he reached out his hand and only touched him, and Diophantus, trying to drive another to despair, himself gave his last gasp.

poems.title: Book XI, 115
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: If you have an enemy, Dionysius, call not down on him the curse of Isis or Harpocrates or of any god who blinds men, but call on Simon and you will see what a god’s power is and what Simon’s is.

poems.title: Book XI, 116
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Lord Caesar, as they tell, Eurystheus once sent down great Heracles to the house of Hades; but now Menophanes the physician has sent me. So let him be called Doctor Eurystheus and no longer Doctor Menophanes.

poems.title: Book XI, 124
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A. Stranger, what dost thou seek to know? B. Who are here in earth under these tombs? A. All those whom Zopyrus robbed of the sweet day-light, Damis, Aristoteles, Demetrius, Arcesilaus, Sostratus, and the next ones so far as Paraetonium. For with a wooden herald’s staff and counterfeit sandals,” like Hermes, he leads down his patients to Hell.

poems.title: Book XI, 162
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: One came to ask the prophet Olympicus if he should take ship for Rhodes and how to sail there safely. And the prophet said, “First have a new ship and don’t start in winter, but in summer. If you do this you will go there and back, unless a pirate catches you at sea.”’

poems.title: Book XI, 169
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Yesterday, Glaucus, Dinarchus the miser being about to hang himself, did not die, poor fellow, all for the sake of sixpence ; for the rope cost sixpence, but he tried to drive a hard bargain, seeking perhaps some other cheap death. This is the very height of wretched avarice, for a man to be dying, Glaucus, and not able to die, poor fellow, all for the sake of sixpence.

poems.title: Book XI, 170
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Philo the miser weeps not because he is dying, but because he paid thirty pounds for his coffin, Let him off this, and as there is room in it, put one of his many little children into it besides.

poems.title: Book XI, 186
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: The night-raven’s song bodes death, but when Demophilus sings the night-raven itself dies.

poems.title: Book XI, 241
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Your mouth and your breech, Theodorus, smell the same, so that it would be a famous task for men of science to distinguish them. You ought really to write on a label which is your mouth and which your breech, but now when you speak I think you break wind.

poems.title: Book XI, 242
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: I can’ tell whether Diodorus is yawning or has broken wind, for he has one breath above and below.

poems.title: Book XI, 243
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Onesimus went to the bath to bathe on the twelfth of the month Dystrus in the year of Antiphilus, leaving at home a child at the breast, whom when he has finished bathing he will find to be the father of two other children. . . . He writes us to say he will go again next year, for the bath-men promise to take off the heat then.

poems.title: Book XI, 251
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A stone-deaf man went to law with another stone-deaf man, and the judge was much deafer than the pair of them. One of them contended that the other owed him five months’ rent, and the other said that his opponent had ground corn at night. Says the judge, looking at them: “ Why are you quarrelling? She is your mother; you must both maintain her.”

poems.title: Book XI, 252
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: If you kiss me you hate me, and if you hate me you kiss me. But if you don’t hate me, dear friend, don’t kiss me!

poems.title: Book XI, 329
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Demonax, do not always turn down your eyes, nor indulge your tongue; the pig has a formidable thorn. And you live... and sleep in Phoenicia, and though not Semele’s son, art nourished by a thigh.

poems.title: Book XI, 330
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: I was invited yesterday, Demetrius, and came to supper to-day. Don’t find fault with me; you have a long staircase. I spent an age on it, and I should not have got safe up it to-day only I came up holding on to a donkey’s tail. You touch the stars: Zeus, it seems, when he ran away with Ganymede, went up with him by this route. But from here how long will it take you to reach Hades? You are not wanting in cleverness; you have hit on a trick for being immortal.

poems.title: Book XI, 331
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Philo had a boat called the “Saviour,” but in it perhaps not even Zeus himself can be saved. Its name only was Saviour, but the passengers sailed either close to land or to Persephone.

poems.title: Book XI, 332
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Icanver the captain embarked us, it seems, on his twenty-oarer, not for a sail, but to bale her out. For the water in her is not little, but Poseidon seems to sail over in her to the opposite shore. It is the first time a ship with the dropsy has been seen. But I, at least, fear lest you may see what was once a long boat turn into our long home.

poems.title: Book XI, 395
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A r—r which cannot find an outlet kills many a man; a f—t also saves, sending forth its lisping music. Therefore if a f—t saves, and on the other hand kills, a f—t has the same power as kings.

poems.title: Book XI, 398
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A man, by dyeing his head, destroyed the hair itself, and his head from being very hairy became all like an egg. The dyer attained this result, that no barber now ever cuts his hair be it white or dark.

poems.title: Book XI, 406
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: I see Nicon’s hooked nose, Menippus, and it is evident that he himself is not far off. Well, he will come; let us wait all the same, for at most he is not, I suppose, more than half a mile from his nose. But it, as you see, comes on in front of him, and if we stand on a high hill we shall get a view of him too.

poems.title: Book XI, 407
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: As lean Menestratus was sitting in spring-time an ant came out and pulled him into a crevice; but a fly flew up and carried him off, just as the eagle carried Ganymede to the heavenly chamber of Zeus. He fell from the fly’s hands, but not even so did he light on the earth, but is hanging by his eyelids from a spider's web.

poems.title: Lost Drink (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: At the Hermaea, Aphrodisius, while lifting six gallons of wine for us, stumbled and dealt us great woe. "From wine also perished the Centaur," and ah that we had too! but now it perished from us.

poems.title: The Popular Singer (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: The night-raven's song is deadly; but when Demophilus sings, the very night-raven dies.

poems.title: Slow and Sure (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Charmus ran for the three miles in Arcadia with five others; surprising to say, he actually came in seventh. When there were only six, perhaps you will say, how seventh? A friend of his went along in his great-coat crying, "Keep it up, Charmus!" and so he arrives seventh; and if only he had had five more friends, Zoïlus, he would have come in twelfth.

poems.title: God and the Doctor (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Marcus the doctor called yesterday on the marble Zeus; though marble, and though Zeus, his funeral is to-day.

poems.title: The Physician and the Astrologer (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Diophantus the asrologer said that Hermogenes the physician had only nine months to live; and he laughing replied, "what Cronus may do in nine months, do you consider; but I can make short work with you." He spoke, and reaching out, just touched him, and Diophantus, while forbidding another to hope, gasped out his own life.

poems.title: Simon the Oculist (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: If you have an enemy, Dionysius, call not down upon him Isis nor Harpocrates, nor whatever god strikes men blind, but Simon; and you will know what God and what Simon can do.

poems.title: Scientific Surgery (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Agclaus killed Acestorides while operating; for, "Poor man," he said, "he would have been lame for life."

poems.title: Soothsaying (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Some one came inquiring of the prophet Olympicus whether he should sail to Rhodes, and how he should have a safe voyage; and the prophet replied, "First have a new ship, and set sail not in winter but in summer; for if you do this you will travel there and back safely, unless a pirate captures you at sea."

poems.title: Cross Purposes (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: A deaf man went to law with a deaf man, and the judge was a long way deafer than both. The one claimed that the other owed him five months' rent; and he replied that he had ground his corn by night; then the judge, looking down on them, said, "Why quarrel? she is your mother; keep her between you."

poems.title: The Patent Stove (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: You have bought a brass hot-water urn, Heliodorus, that is chillier than the north wind about Thrace; do not blow, do not labour, you but raise smoke in vain; it is a brass wine-cooler you have bought against summer.

poems.title: The Lifeboat (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Philo had a boat, the Salvation, but not Zeus himself, I believe, can be safe in her; for she was salvation in name only, and those who got on board her used either to go aground or to go underground.

poems.title: Nicon's Nose (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I see Nicon's hooked nose, Menippus; it is evident he is not far off now; oh, he will be here, let us just wait; for at the most his nose is not, I fancy, five stadia off him. Nay, here it is, you see, stepping forward; if we stand on a high mound we shall catch sight of him in person.

poems.title: The Use of Life (Mackail)
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Must I not die? what matters it to me whether I depart to Hades gouty or fleet of foot? for many will carry me; let me become lame, for hardly on their account need I ever cease from revelling.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.38: εὐμεγέθης πείθει με καλὴ γυνή, ἄν
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
εὐμεγέθης πείθει με καλὴ γυνή, ἄν τε καὶ ἀκμῆς
ἅπτητʼ, ἄν τε καὶ ᾖ, Σιμύλε, πρεσβυτέρη.
ἡ μὲν γάρ με νέα περιλήψεται, ἡ δὲ παλαιὴ
γραῖά με καὶ ῥυσή, Σιμύλε, λειχάσεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.39: οὐκ ἀποθνῄσκειν δεῖ με; τί μοι
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
οὐκ ἀποθνῄσκειν δεῖ με; τί μοι μέλει, ἤν τε ποδαγρὸς
ἤν τε δρομεὺς γεγονὼς εἰς Ἀίδην ὑπάγω;
πολλοὶ γάρ μʼ ἀροῦσιν. ἔα χωλόν με γενέσθαι·
τῶνδʼ ἕνεκεν γὰρ ἴδʼ ὡς οὔποτʼ ἐῶ θιάσους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.40: τῆς μητρὸς μὴ ἄκουε, Φιλουμένη· ἢν
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τῆς μητρὸς μὴ ἄκουε, Φιλουμένη· ἢν γὰρ ἀπέλθω
καὶ θῶ ἅπαξ ἔξω τὸν πόδα τῆς πόλεως,
τῶν καταπαιζόντων μὴ σχῇς λόγον, ἀλλὰ γʼ ἐκείνοις
ἐμπαίξασ’, ἄρξαι πλεῖον ἐμοῦ τι ποεῖν
πάντα λίθον κίνει. σαυτὴν τρέφε, καὶ γράφε πρός με
εἰς ποίην ἀκτὴν εὐφρόσυνον γέγονας.
εὐτακτεῖν πειρῶ· τὸ δʼ ἐνοίκιον, ἤν τι περισσὸν
γίνηται, καὶ ἐμοὶ φρόντισον ἱμάτιον.
ἢν ἐν γαστρὶ λάβῃς, τέκε, ναὶ τέκε μὴ θορυβηθῇς·
εὑρήσει πόθεν ἔστʼ, ἐλθὸν ἐς ἡλικίην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.31: Αἰγιβάτῃ τόδε Πανὶ, καὶ εὐκάρπῳ Διονύσῳ,
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
Αἰγιβάτῃ τόδε Πανὶ, καὶ εὐκάρπῳ Διονύσῳ,
καὶ Δηοῖ Χθονίῃ ξυνὸν ἔθηκα γέρας.
αἰτέομαι δʼ αὐτοὺς καλὰ πώεα καὶ καλὸν οἶνον,
καὶ καλὸν ἀμῆσαι καρπὸν ἀπʼ ἀσταχύων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.285: ἡ πρὶν Ἀθηναίης ὑπὸ κερκίσι καὶ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
ἡ πρὶν Ἀθηναίης ὑπὸ κερκίσι καὶ τὰ καθʼ ἱστῶν
νήματα Νικαρέτη πολλὰ μιτωσαμένη,
Κύπριδι τὸν κάλαθον τά τε πηνία καὶ τὰ σὺν αὐτοῖς
ἄρμενʼ ἐπὶ προδόμου πάντα πυρῆς ἔθετο,
ἔρρετε, φωνήσασα, “ κακῶν λιμηρὰ γυναικῶν
ἔργα, νέον τήκειν ἄνθος ἐπιστάμενα.”
εἵλετο δὲ στεφάνους καὶ πηκτίδα καὶ μετὰ κώμων
ἡ παῖς τερπνὸν ἔχειν ἐν θαλίαις βίοτον
εἶπε δέ· “παντός σοι δεκάτην ἀπὸ λήμματος οἴσω,
Κύπρι σὺ δʼ ἐργασίην καὶ λάβε καὶ μετάδος.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.159: Ὀρφεὺς μὲν κιθάρᾳ πλεῖστον γέρας εἵλετο
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
Ὀρφεὺς μὲν κιθάρᾳ πλεῖστον γέρας εἵλετο θνητῶν,
Νέστωρ δὲ γλώσσης ἡδυλόγου σοφίῃ,
τεκτοσύνῃ δʼ ἐπέων πολυίστωρ θεῖος Ὅμηρος,
Τηλεφάνης δʼ αὐλοῖς, οὗ τάφος ἐστὶν ὅδε.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.330: α. κράνας εὐύδρου παρὰ νάμασι καὶ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
α. κράνας εὐύδρου παρὰ νάμασι καὶ παρὰ Νύμφαις,
ἔστασέν με Σίμων, Πᾶνα τὸν αἰγιπόδην.
β.  τεῦ δὲ χάριν; α. λέξω τοι· ὅσον ποθέεις ἀπὸ κράνας
καὶ πίε, καὶ κοίλαν κάλπιν ἑλὼν ἄρυσαι·
ποσσὶ δὲ μὴ ποτὶ νίπτρα φέρειν κρυστάλλινα  Νυμφᾶν
δῶρα, τὸν ὑβριστὰν εἰς ἐμὲ δερκόμενος.
β. ὦ σέμνʼ — - α. οὐ λέξεις ἕτερον λόγον, ἀλλὰ παρέξεις
πυγίξαι· τούτοις χρῶμαι ὁ Πὰν νομίμοις.
ἢν δὲ ποιῇς ἐπίτηδες, ἔχων πάθος, ἔστι καὶ ἄλλα
τέχνα· τῷ ῥοπάλῳ τὰν κεφαλὰν λέπομες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.576: παρθένε Τριτογένεια, τί τὴν Κύπριν ἄρτι
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
παρθένε Τριτογένεια, τί τὴν Κύπριν ἄρτι με λυπεῖς,
ἁρπάξασα δʼ ἐμὸν δῶρον ἔχεις παλάμῃ;
μέμνησαι τὸ πάροιθεν ἐν Ἰδαίοις σκοπέλοισιν
ὡς Πάρις οὐ σὲ καλήν, ἀλλʼ ἔμʼ ἐδογμάτισεν.
σὸν δόρυ καὶ σάκος ἐστὶν ἐμὸν δὲ τὸ μῆλον ὑπάρχει·
ἀρκεῖ τῷ μήλῳ κεῖνος ὁ πρὶν πόλεμος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.1: Ἑρμαίοις ἡμῖν Ἀφροδίσιος ἓξ χόας οἴνου
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
Ἑρμαίοις ἡμῖν Ἀφροδίσιος ἓξ χόας οἴνου
αἴρων, προσκόψας πένθος ἔθηκε μέγα.
οἶνος καὶ Κένταυρον ἀπώλεσεν ὡς ὄφελεν δὲ
χἠμᾶς· νῦν δʼ ἡμεῖς τοῦτον ἀπωλέσαμεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.7: οὐδεὶς τὴν ἰδίην συνεχῶς, Χαρίδημε, γυναῖκα
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
οὐδεὶς τὴν ἰδίην συνεχῶς, Χαρίδημε, γυναῖκα
βινεῖν  ἐκ ψυχῆς τερπόμενος δύναται·
οὕτως ἡ φύσις ἐστὶ φιλόκνισος, ἀλλοτριόχρως,
καὶ ζητεῖ διόλου τὴν ξενοκυσθαπάτην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.17: ἦν Στέφανος πτωχὸς κηπεὺς θʼ ἅμα·
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
ἦν Στέφανος πτωχὸς κηπεὺς θʼ ἅμα· νῦν δὲ προκόψας
πλουτεῖ, καὶ γεγένητʼ εὐθὺ Φιλοστέφανος,
τέσσαρα τῷ πρώτῳ Στεφάνῳ καλὰ γράμματα προσθείς·
ἔσται δʼ εἰς ὥρας Ἱπποκρατιππιάδης,
ἢ διὰ τὴν σπατάλην Διονυσιοπηγανόδωρος·
ἐν δʼ ἀγορανομίῳ παντὶ μένει Στέφανος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.18: οὐκ ἐν ʽγαστρὶ λαβοῦσα Φιλαίνιον Ἡλιοδώρῳ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
οὐκ ἐν ʽγαστρὶ λαβοῦσα Φιλαίνιον Ἡλιοδώρῳ
θήλειαν τίκτει παῖδʼ ἀπὸ ταὐτομάτου.
τοῦ δʼ ἐπὶ θηλείῃ λυπουμένου, ἓξ διαλείπει
ἤματα, καὶ τίκτειν ἄρσενα παῖδʼ ἔφατο.
οὕτως Βούβαστις καταλύεται· εἰ γὰρ ἑκάστη
τέξεται ὡς αὐτή, τίς  θεοῦ ἐστι λόγος;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.71: ἤκμασε Νικονόη· κἀγὼ λέγω· ἤκμασε δʼ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
ἤκμασε Νικονόη· κἀγὼ λέγω· ἤκμασε δʼ αὐτή
ἡνίκα Δευκαλίων ἄπλετον εἶδεν ὕδωρ.
ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ἡμεῖς οὐκ οἴδαμεν, ἀλλʼ ὅτι ταύτην
οὐκ ἄνδρα ζητεῖν νῦν ἔδει, ἀλλὰ τάφον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.73: γραῖα καλὴ ʽτί γάρ;ʼ οἶσθας ὅτʼ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
γραῖα καλὴ ʽτί  γάρ;ʼ οἶσθας ὅτʼ ἦν νέα· ἀλλὰ τότʼ ᾔτει,
νῦν δʼ ἐθέλει δοῦναι μισθὸν ἐλαυνομένη.
εὑρήσεις τεχνῖτιν ὅταν δὲ πίῃ, τότε μᾶλλον
εἰς ὃ θέλεις αὐτὴν εὐεπίτακτον ἔχεις.
πίνει γὰρ καὶ τρεῖς καὶ τέσσαρας, ἢν ἐθελήσῃς,
ξέστας, κἀκ τούτου γίνετʼ ἄνω τὰ κάτω·
κολλᾶται, κνίζει, παθικεύεται· ἤν τι διδῷ τις,
λαμβάνει· ἢν μὴ δῷ, μισθὸν ἔχει τὸ πάθος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.74: τὴν δύσκωφον γραῖαν, Ὀνήσιμε, πρὸς Διός,
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τὴν δύσκωφον γραῖαν, Ὀνήσιμε, πρὸς Διός, ἔξω
ἔκβαλε· πολλὰ λίην πράγματά μοι παρέχει.
ἢν αὐτῇ τυροὺς ἁπαλοὺς εἴπωμεν ἐνέγκαι,
οὐ τυρούς, πυροὺς δʼ ἔρχετʼ ἔχουσα νέους.
πρῴην τὴν κεφαλὴν ἐπόνουν, καὶ πήγανον αὐτὴν
ᾔτουν ἡ δʼ ἔφερεν τήγανον ὀστράκινον.
ἂν †   ὀπὸν αἰτήσω, δοκὸν εἰσφέρει· ἄν, λάχανόν μοι.
εἴπω δὸς  πεινῶν, εὐθὺ φέρει λάσανον.
ὄξος ἐὰν αἰτῶ, τόξον φέρει· ἂν δέ γε τόξον,
ὄξος· ὅλως δʼ ὃ λέγω οὔποτʼ ἐπαισθάνεται.
αἰσχρὸν τῆς γραός με χάριν κήρυκα γενέσθαι,
καὶ μελετᾶν ἔξω, νυκτὸς ἐγειρόμενον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.82: πέντε μετʼ ἄλλων Χάρμος ἐν Ἀρκαδίᾳ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
πέντε μετʼ ἄλλων Χάρμος ἐν Ἀρκαδίᾳ δολιχεύων,
θαῦμα μέν, ἀλλʼ ὄντως ἕβδομος ἐξέπεσεν.
ἓξ ὄντων, τάχʼ ἐρεῖς, πῶς ἕβδομος ; εἷς  φίλος αὐτοῦ,
θάρσει, Χάρμε, λέγων, ἦλθεν ἐν ἱματίῳ.
ἕβδομος οὖν οὕτω παραγίνεται· εἰ δʼ ἔτι πέντε
εἶχε φίλους, ἦλθʼ ἄν, Ζωίλε, δωδέκατος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.96: Ἀρκάδας οὐχ οὕτω Στυμφαλίδες, ὡς ἐμὲ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
Ἀρκάδας οὐχ οὕτω Στυμφαλίδες, ὡς ἐμὲ κίχλαι
αἱ νέκυες ξηροῖς ἤκαχον ὀσταρίοις,
ἅρπυιαι, δραχμῆς ξηρὴ δεκάς. ὦ ἐλεειναὶ
λειμώνων ἐτύμως, ἔρρετε, νυκτερίδες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.110: τρεῖς λεπτοὶ πρῴην περὶ λεπτοσύνης ἐμάχοντο,
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τρεῖς λεπτοὶ πρῴην περὶ λεπτοσύνης ἐμάχοντο,
τίς  προκριθεὶς εἴη λεπτεπιλεπτότερος.
ὧν ὁ μὲν εἷς,Ἕρμων, μεγάλην ἐνεδείξατο τέχνην,
καὶ διέδυ ῥαφίδος τρῆμα, λίνον κατέχων
Δημᾶς δʼ ἐκ τρώγλης βαίνων ἐς ἀράχνιον ἔστη,
ἡ δʼ ἀράχνη νήθουσ’ αὐτὸν ἀπεκρέμασεν.
Σωσίπατρος δʼ ἐβόησεν “ ἐμὲ στεφανώσατʼ ἐγὼ
εἰ βλέπομʼ, ἥττημαι· πνεῦμα γάρ εἰμι μόνον.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.124: α. ξεῖνε, τί μὰν πεύθῃ; β.
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
α. ξεῖνε, τί μὰν πεύθῃ; β. τίνες ἐν χθονὶ τοῖσδʼ ὑπὸ τύμβοις;
α. οὓς γλυκεροῦ φέγγους Ζώπυρος ἐστέρισεν,
Δᾶμις, Ἀριστοτέλης, Δημήτριος, Ἀρκεσίλαος,
Σώστρατος, οἵ τʼ ὀπίσω μέχρι Παραιτονίου.
κηρύκιον γὰρ ἔχων ξύλινον, καὶ πλαστὰ πέδιλα,
ὡς Ἑρμῆς, κατάγει τοὺς θεραπευομένους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.162: εἰς Ῥόδον εἰ πλεύσει τις Ὀλυμπικὸν
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
εἰς Ῥόδον εἰ πλεύσει τις Ὀλυμπικὸν ἦλθεν ἐρωτῶν
τὸν μάντιν, καὶ πῶς πλεύσεται ἀσφαλέως.
χὠ μάντις, πρῶτον μέν, ἔφη, “ καινὴν ἔχε τὴν ναῦν,
καὶ μὴ χειμῶνος, τοῦ δὲ θέρους ἀνάγου.
τοῦτο γὰρ ἂν ποιῇς, ἥξεις κἀκεῖσε καὶ ὧδε,
ἂν μὴ πειρατὴς ἐν πελάγει σε λάβῃ.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.169: ἐχθὲς ἀπάγχεσθαι μέλλων Δείναρχος ὁ φείδων,
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
ἐχθὲς ἀπάγχεσθαι μέλλων Δείναρχος ὁ φείδων,
Γλαῦκε, διʼ ἓξ χαλκοῦς δύσμορος οὐκ ἔθανεν
ἓξ χαλκῶν ἦν γὰρ τὸ σχοινίον· ἀλλʼ ἐδυσώνει,
εὔωνον ζητῶν ἄλλον ἴσως θάνατον.
τοῦτο φιλαργυρίας δεινῆς ὅρος, ὃς γʼ ἀποθνῄσκων,
Γλαῦκε, διʼ ἓξ χαλκοῦς δύσμορος οὐκ ἔθανεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.170: δακρύει Φείδων ὁ φιλάργυρος, οὐχ ὅτι
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
δακρύει Φείδων ὁ φιλάργυρος, οὐχ ὅτι θνῄσκει,
ἀλλʼ ὅτι πέντε μνῶν τὴν σορὸν ἐπρίατο.
τοῦτʼ αὐτῷ χαρίσασθε, καί, ὡς τόπος ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτῇ,
τῶν πολλῶν τεκνίων ἕν τι προσεμβάλετε.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.186: νυκτικόραξ ᾄδει θανατηφόρον ἀλλʼ ὅταν ᾅσῃ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
νυκτικόραξ ᾄδει θανατηφόρον ἀλλʼ ὅταν ᾅσῃ
Δημόφιλος, θνήσκει καὐτὸς ὁ νυκτικόραξ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.241: τὸ στόμα χὠ πρωκτὸς ταὐτόν, Θεόδωρε,
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τὸ στόμα χὠ πρωκτὸς ταὐτόν, Θεόδωρε, σοῦ ὄζει,
ὥστε διαγνῶναι τοῖς φυσικοῖς καλὸν ἦν.
ἦ γράψαι σε ἔδει ποῖον στόμα, ποῖον ὁ πρωκτός.
νῦν δὲ λαλοῦντός σου βδεῖν σ’ ἐνόμιζον ἐγώ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.242: οὐ δύναμαι γνῶναι, πότερον χαίνει Διόδωρος,
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
οὐ δύναμαι γνῶναι, πότερον χαίνει Διόδωρος,
ἢ βδῆσ’· ἓν γὰρ ἔχει πνεῦμα κάτω καὶ ἄνω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.243: λούσασθαι πεπόρευται Ὀνήσιμος εἰς βαλανεῖον
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
λούσασθαι πεπόρευται Ὀνήσιμος εἰς βαλανεῖον
δωδεκάτῃ δύστρου μηνός, ἐπʼ Ἀντιφίλου,
παῖδα λιπὼν οἴκοις ἐπιτίτθιον, ὃν δύο τέκνων
ἄλλων εὑρήσει λουσάμενος πατέρα.
ἥξειν δʼ εἰς ὥρας ἡμῖν γράφει· οἱ βαλανεῖς γὰρ
εἰς τότε τάσσονται τὴν πυρίαν καθελεῖν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.251: Δυσκώφῳ δύσκωφος ἐκρίνετο· καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
Δυσκώφῳ δύσκωφος ἐκρίνετο· καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον
ἦν ὁ κριτὴς τούτων τῶν δύο κωφότερος.
ὧν ὁ μὲν ἀντέλεγεν τὸ ἐνοίκιον αὐτὸν ὀφείλειν
μηνῶν πένθʼ  ὁ δʼ ἔφη νυκτὸς ἀληλεκέναι.
ἐμβλέψας δʼ αὐτοῖς ὁ κριτὴς λέγει, “ἐς τί μάχεσθε;
μήτηρ ἔσθʼ ὑμῶν ἀμφότεροι τρέφετε.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.252: εἴ με φιλεῖς, μισεῖς με· καὶ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
εἴ με φιλεῖς, μισεῖς με· καὶ εἰ μισεῖς, σύ φιλεῖς με·
εἰ δέ με μὴ μισεῖς, φίλτατε, μή με φίλει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.329: Δημῶναξ, μὴ πάντα κάτω βλέπε, μηδὲ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
Δημῶναξ, μὴ πάντα κάτω βλέπε, μηδὲ χαρίζου
τῇ γλώσσῃ· δεινὴν χοῖρος ἄκανθαν ἔχει.
καὶ σὺ ζῇς †    ἡμῖν, ἐν Φοινίκῃ δὲ καθεύδεις,
κοὐκ ὢν ἐκ Σεμέλης μηροτραφὴς γέγονας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.330: ἐκλήθην ἐχθές, Δημήτριε· σήμερον ἦλθον
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
ἐκλήθην ἐχθές, Δημήτριε· σήμερον ἦλθον
δειπνεῖν. μὴ μέμψῃ, κλίμακʼ ἔχεις μεγάλην
ἐν ταύτᾐ πεποίηκα πολὺν χρόνον οὐδʼ ἂν ἐσώθην
σήμερον, ἀλλʼ ἀνέβην κέρκον ὄνου κατέχων.
ἧψαι τῶν ἄστρων Ζεὺς ἡνίκα τὸν Γανυμήδην
ἥρπασε, τῇδʼ αὐτόν, φαίνετʼ, ἔχων ἀνέβη.
ἔνθεν δʼ εἰς Ἀίδην ποτʼ ἀφίξεαι; οὐκ ἀφυὴς εἶ
εὕρηκας τέχνην πῶς ἒσῃ ἀθάνατος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.331: εἶχε Φίλων λέμβον Σωτήριχον ἀλλʼ ἐν
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
εἶχε Φίλων λέμβον Σωτήριχον ἀλλʼ ἐν ἐκείνῳ
σωθῆνʼ οὐδὲ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ἴσως δύναται.
οὔνομα γὰρ μόνον ἦν Σωτήριχος, οἱ δʼ ἐπιβάντες
ἔπλεον ἢ παρὰ γῆν, ἢ παρὰ Φερσεφόνην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.332: οὐ πλεῖν, ἀλλʼ ἀντλεῖν ἡμᾶς Εἴκανδρος
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
οὐ πλεῖν, ἀλλʼ ἀντλεῖν ἡμᾶς Εἴκανδρος ὁ πρωρεὺς
εἰς τὴν εἰκόσορον φαίνεται ἐμβιβάσας·
οὐκ ὀλίγον γὰρ ἔνεστιν ὕδωρ ἔσω, ἀλλʼ ὁ Ποσειδῶν
ἐν ταύτῃ διαπλεῖν φαίνεται εἰς τὸ πέραν
νῦν πρῶτον ναῦς ὦπται ὑδρωπική, ἀλλά γε [ δείδω]
μὴ σορὸν οὖσαν ἴδῃς τὴν πάλαι εἰκόσορον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.395: πορδὴ ἀποκτέννει πολλοὺς ἀδιέξοδος οὖσα·
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
πορδὴ ἀποκτέννει πολλοὺς ἀδιέξοδος οὖσα·
πορδὴ καὶ σῴζει τραυλὸν ἱεῖσα μέλος.
οὐκοῦν εἰ σῴζει, καὶ ἀποκτέννει πάλι πορδή,
τοῖς βασιλεῦσιν ἴσην πορδὴ ἔχει δύναμιν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.398: τὴν κεφαλὴν βάπτων τις ἀπώλεσε τὰς
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τὴν κεφαλὴν βάπτων τις ἀπώλεσε τὰς τρίχας αὐτὰς,
καὶ δασὺς ὢν λίαν, ᾠὸν ἅπας γέγονεν.
τοῦτο βαφεὺς ἐπόησε, τὸ μηκέτι κουρέα τέμνειν
μήτε κόμην λευκὴν μήτε μελαινομένην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.406: τοῦ γρυποῦ Νίκωνος ὁρῶ τὴν ῥῖνα,
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τοῦ γρυποῦ Νίκωνος ὁρῶ τὴν ῥῖνα, Μένιππε·
αὐτὸς δʼ οὐ μακρὰν φαίνεται εἶναι ἔτι.
πλὴν ἥξει, μείνωμεν ὅμως· εἰ γὰρ πολύ, πέντε
τῆς ῥινὸς σταδίους, οἴομαι, οὐκ ἀπέχει.
ἀλλʼ αὐτὴ μέν, ὁρᾷς, προπορεύεται· ἢν δʼ ἐπὶ βουνὸν
ὑψηλὸν στῶμεν, καὐτὸν ἐσοψόμεθα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.407: τὸν λεπτὸν θακεῦντα Μενέστρατον εἴαρος ὥρῃ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τὸν λεπτὸν θακεῦντα Μενέστρατον εἴαρος ὥρῃ
μύρμηξ ἐξελθὼν εἵλκυσεν εἰς ῥαγάδα·
μυῖα δʼ ἐπιπτᾶσ’ αὐτὸν ἀνήρπασεν, ὡς Γανυμήδη
αἰετὸς εἰς θαλάμους οὐρανίους Κρονίδεω·
πίπτεν δʼ ἐκ χειρῶν μυίης, κοὐδʼ ὣς θίγε γαίης,
ἐκ δʼ ἀράχνης ἱστοῦ τῶν βλεφάρων κρέμαται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.166: τὴν γοεραῖς πνεύσασαν ἐν ὠδίνεσσι Λαμίσκην
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τὴν γοεραῖς πνεύσασαν ἐν ὠδίνεσσι Λαμίσκην
ὕστατα, Νικαρέτης παῖδα καὶ Εὐπόλιδος,
σὺν βρέφεσιν διδύμοις, Σαμίην γένος, αἱ παρὰ Νείλῳ
κρύπτουσιν Λιβύης ᾐόνες εἰκοσέτιν.
ἀλλά, κόραι, τῇ παιδὶ λεχώια δῶρα φέρουσαι,
θερμὰ κατὰ ψυχροῦ δάκρυα χεῖτε τάφου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.102: ἐξαίρων ποτʼ ἄκανθαν ὁ λεπτακινὸς Διόδωρος
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
ἐξαίρων ποτʼ ἄκανθαν ὁ λεπτακινὸς Διόδωρος
αὐτὸς ἐτρύπησεν τῷ ποδὶ τὴν βελόνην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.328: τὴν μίαν Ἑρμογένης κἀγώ ποτε καὶ
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τὴν μίαν Ἑρμογένης κἀγώ ποτε καὶ Κλεόβουλος
ἤγομεν εἰς κοινὴν κύπριν Ἀριστοδίκην·
ἧς ἔλαχον μὲν ἐγὼ πολιὴν ἅλα ναιέμεν αὐτός·
εἷς γὰρ ἕν, οὐ πάντες πάντα, διειλόμεθα.
Ἑρμογένης δʼ ἔλαχε στυγερὸν δόμον εὐρώεντα,
ὕστατον, εἰς ἀφανῆ χῶρον ὑπερχόμενος,
ἔνθʼ ἀκταὶ νεκύων, καὶ ἐρινεοὶ ἠνεμόεντες
δινεῦνται πνοιῇ δυσκελάδων ἀνέμων.
Ζῆνα δὲ θὲς Κλεόβουλον, ὃς οὐρανὸν εἰσαναβαίνειν,
τὸ ψολόεν κατέχων ἐν χερὶ πῦρ, ἔλαχεν.
γῆ δʼ ἔμενε ξυνὴ πάντων ψίαθον γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ
στρώσαντες, τὴν γραῦν ὧδε διειλόμεθα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.415: τίς σοῦ, Μεντορίδη, προφανῶς οὕτως μετέθηκεν
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text:
τίς  σοῦ, Μεντορίδη, προφανῶς οὕτως μετέθηκεν
τὴν πυγήν, οὗπερ τὸ στόμʼ ἔκειτο πρὸ τοῦ;
βδεῖς γάρ, κοὐκ ἀναπνεῖς, φθέγγῃ δʼ ἐκ τῶν καταγείω
θαῦμὰ μʼ ἔχει τὰ κάτω πῶς σου ἄνω γέγονεν.
